title: Sell Mineral Rights in Dillonvale, OH
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Dillonvale, OH
metaDescription: Dillonvale sits in Jefferson County, a former coal-mining village where old mineral severances are common. See what that means before you sell.
heroLead: Dillonvale grew up as a coal-mining village, and those coal-era land deals are exactly why so many mineral interests here need a title search before anyone can talk price.
intro: Dillonvale is a small village in Jefferson County that grew up around coal mining in the late 1800s and early 1900s, and much of the land in and around it changed hands through mining-company transactions that often severed oil, gas and coal rights separately from the surface. Sitting on the Utica flank rather than the deep core, the area hasn't seen the drilling density of counties like Harrison or Belmont, but Marcellus proximity from across the Ohio River adds another layer to what any given tract's minerals might be worth.

sections.heading: Coal-era severances and what they mean today
paragraphs: When a mining company bought land around Dillonvale a century ago, the deed often reserved coal rights for the company while leaving oil and gas with the original farm family, or split all three separately among different parties entirely. That means your mineral interest may be entirely disconnected from who owns the coal or the surface today, and figuring out which deed actually controls your oil and gas rights requires tracing the chain of title at the Jefferson County Recorder's office in Steubenville.

sections.heading: Flank-position value considerations
paragraphs: Because this part of Jefferson County sits toward the edge of the Utica core, whether your tract has ever been leased or drilled matters more here than it might in a heavily developed county. An unleased, undrilled interest is priced conservatively against comparable recent activity, while a producing interest with royalty history behind it gives a buyer real numbers to work from.

faqs.question: How do I know if coal rights and oil and gas rights were severed separately on my land?
faqs.answer: The original severance deed will spell this out, and it's worth pulling directly from the Jefferson County Recorder rather than assuming from what a neighbor's deed says, since terms varied by transaction.

faqs.question: Is there Marcellus activity near Dillonvale?
faqs.answer: Jefferson County borders the West Virginia panhandle where Marcellus development has been extensive, so some tracts in this part of the county have drawn interest tied to that formation as well as Utica.

faqs.question: What if my family's interest has never produced any royalty?
faqs.answer: That's common for older severed interests in this area. Value in that case depends on your net mineral acres and nearby activity rather than existing production history, and it's worth confirming the interest is still intact under Ohio law.

faqs.question: What paperwork helps a buyer give me an accurate range?
faqs.answer: Your deed or severance instrument, any lease or division order, and recent royalty statements if you receive them. Those establish net mineral acres and decimal interest, which is what a real number is built on.
